chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father, from al-Nawfali, from al-Sakuni, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
"Do not bear witness with a testimony that you do not remember, for whoever wishes can write a document and carve a seal."

Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id said: Ja'far ibn 'Isa wrote to him: 'I am your ransom. Neighbors of ours came to me with a document, claiming that they were testifying me regarding what is in it. My name was in the document in my own handwriting, which I recognized, but I did not remember the testimony. They invited me to it, so should I testify for them regarding my knowledge that my name is in the document, while I do not remember the testimony? Or is the testimony not obligatory upon them until I remember it? Whether my name was in the document in my handwriting or not?' So he wrote: 'Do not bear witness.'

key_terms.تَذْكُرُهَا: You remember it (referring to the content of the testimony)

ai.seo_question: What is the condition for a valid witness testimony in Shia jurisprudence regarding memory of the content?
ai.summary: This hadith from the chapter on *Bayyināt* (evidence) clarifies the distinction between recognizing a signature and bearing substantive witness, a critical nuance in Shia jurisprudence regarding the validity of testimony. The Imam’s concise ruling, 'Do not bear witness,' underscores that legal testimony requires conscious recall of the specific act, preventing errors in judicial records where names might be authenticated without knowledge of the underlying facts. This principle safeguards the integrity of *Shahādah* by ensuring it is an active, knowledgeable affirmation rather than a passive acknowledgment of identity.
